# Maintaining the skills

Read this before changing anything under a `skills/` directory. It is not loaded automatically:
`AGENTS.md` points here so that a description of what the skills are expected to do stays out of
the context of eval runs (see `eval-tools/README.md`).

## Shared contract

- **Record, don't invent** is the shared contract across every skill: a skill states as fact only what the user or the repository established, and a gap is never filled with a guess. What a skill does with the gap depends on what it delivers. The skills that write a document or a diagram (`adr`, `design-doc`, `structurizr`, `mermaid-sequence`) ask: when the request is too vague to fill the sections honestly, they ask 2–4 targeted questions instead of fabricating, and the questions are the deliverable. Every other skill states its own form of the contract in its note below, and a new skill does the same instead of being added here as an exception.
- **Validation tooling**: today no skill uses an MCP at all, and `adr`, `design-doc`, `unslop`, `code-comments`, `explain` and `technical-writing` use no external tooling: `structurizr` validates, previews, and exports through the `structurizr/structurizr` Docker image (PNG/SVG only through its `<version>-playwright` variant; the regular image refuses them), and `mermaid-sequence` validates through the `minlag/mermaid-cli` Docker image with a local `mmdc` as fallback. Without Docker (or the CLI), both ship the artifact with an explicit "not validated" notice plus the command to run later — **never an install attempt, never a remote validator**.

## Per-skill notes

- **adr** — adr-tools-compatible decision log (`NNNN-slug.md`, `doc/adr` default, `.adr-dir` override, `adr init`-style seed on fresh logs, supersede/amend by editing the *old* ADR's Status section only — ADRs are otherwise immutable). The slug is ASCII-only, as adr-tools' own pipeline computes it on Linux (`tr -Ccs [:alnum:] -`): an accented letter becomes a hyphen (`decisões` → `decis-es`), never transliterated and never kept. Modern spelling `Superseded`/`Supersedes` on write; legacy `Superceded` recognized on read. Tool-parsed scaffolding (adr-tools' `Date:` label, the `## Status/Context/Decision/Consequences` headings, status words, supersede/amend verbs) stays canonical English even in a non-English log, because Structurizr's `!adrs` importer and `adr generate` parse those literals; only the prose is translated. A scope check up front hands an open design to `design-doc`, refuses to record a choice not yet made, and leaves `!adrs` wiring to `structurizr`. Since 1.5.0 the writing step (step 3; step 4 before 1.6.0) applies the `unslop` skill when it is installed, to the title text and section bodies of the record being written; scaffolding, the seed, and every existing record are out of its reach. Since 1.6.0 the third ingredient of a record is the *trade-off* (what the decision gives up in exchange for what it gets: an alternative passed over, a cost, a constraint), not a negative consequence: when the user gives none the skill asks once what was given up, never supplies one, and when the answer is that there was none it writes the record without one and says so in the reply (eval 12). What a no-skill baseline already does on sonnet and what it does not is in `adr-workspace/iteration-17/README.md`; read it before cutting anything from this skill. Whether the skill is reached when the log is in the project, which the trigger harness cannot show, was probed on 2026-11-22 (`adr-workspace/trigger-evals/in-project-2026-11-22/`, claude-sonnet-5-5, `adr` and `unslop` loaded as plugins from outside the project, the prompt alone): 16 of 16 sessions invoked it, always as the first tool call, on a supersede, on a log with `.adr-dir`, and on two requests that never say "ADR".
- **design-doc** — writes, reviews *and* updates design docs via interactive discovery; trade-offs are mandatory (zero-cons = red flag). A change with no choice left open gets no doc: the skill says so and asks once, writing a terse mini-doc only when the team's process requires one. A doc whose design changed is edited in place until the system ships; after that its body is left alone and the change goes into a linked amendment (`Amended by` in the original's header is the only edit). Invention by *consequence* is named in the contract: a fact cannot be asserted in one section and asked in Open questions. The "do nothing" alternative is still always written, but only from the pain the user described; with none described it becomes a question. A user-supplied or house template **governs** (its sections become required); only without a template are sections suggestions. A review still asks the author for a template reference (templates live outside the repo), but the template is context, not a checklist: the review **never audits section presence** — it analyzes only the sections the author wrote, and proposes a section only when the existing content calls for one, as a suggestion tied to that content, in the house template's terms when known and the default catalog's otherwise. Diagram convention: the C4 architecture is authored as **Structurizr DSL** (delegating to the `structurizr` skill when present), embedded as a **PNG/SVG image reference with the DSL folded in a `<details>` block** — render via structurizr's `-playwright` image export when reachable, otherwise leave a placeholder with a one-line "render in the manual pass" note; sequence flows stay Mermaid. No "not machine-validated" disclaimer — manual review is assumed; only a *validation* disclaimer is banned. Generated prose is plain active-voice and gets a spelling pass in self-review. Since 1.6.0 the write step also applies the `unslop` skill when it is installed, to the prose written in that turn only; the two prose bullets of step 3 stay as the floor for an install without it (iteration-26 measured their effect), and a review never runs the author's text through it. 1.7.0 made the write step apply the `technical-writing` skill first, when installed, to the same prose and under the same limits, on the argument that it looks each actor up in the repository, which `unslop` cannot do because it removes and never supplies. 1.8.0 takes that call out and is 1.6.0's `SKILL.md` byte for byte, because the one measurement of it found nothing it adds: `design-doc-workspace/iteration-27/` (2026-11-22, claude-sonnet-5-5, two runs per cell, the three skills installed in a project outside the repository and the prompt given alone) compared 1.7.0 with 1.6.0 on evals 1, 4, 6, 7 and 9, and its checks do not separate them: 98/104 against 98/104 on evals 1, 4 and 6, with 0 to 4 agentless passives per document in both versions. The check written for what the change claims, no actor named that nobody established, is met in 6 of 10 documents with 1.6.0 and in 4 of 10 with 1.7.0, and in one 1.7.0 document the pass itself supplied the actor ("não foram discutidos" became "O time ainda não discutiu"). 1.7.0 invoked `technical-writing` in 9 of 10 runs that wrote a document, read its file without invoking it in the tenth, and cost about 29% more tokens and 15% more US$ per document. Two runs measure no rate, and the judge could tell the version from every 1.7.0 reply. The author decided on that evidence to go back, so 1.8.0 was not run again: its text is the `v160` cell of that iteration. Do not put the call back without a check that separates the versions. The same iteration found that the prompt alone does not reach the write step on evals 7 and 9. On eval 7 both versions ask first and write no file. On eval 9 the description of 1.8.0 and earlier did not win the request: with the plugins loaded from outside the project, sixteen sessions given "…mudou onde os arquivos gerados ficam… Atualiza a documentação." for a shipped design doc invoked no skill and all sixteen rewrote the body of the approved document, while two canary sessions on eval 6 invoked `design-doc` (`technical-writing-workspace/trigger-evals/border-design-doc-2026-11-22/`, 2026-11-22, claude-sonnet-5-5). The lifecycle rule of 1.5.0 (amend a shipped doc, never rewrite it) was therefore reached only when the user named the skill; the description quoted requests to write and to review and none to update. 1.9.0 adds "update" to the opening verbs of the description and one clause in the form of `code-comments` 1.1.0: it names the request, says that it looks like a plain edit and is not one, and says to consult the skill before touching a design doc. With that text loaded as a plugin, eight of eight sessions on the same request invoked `design-doc` and none touched the body of the approved document (`design-doc-workspace/trigger-evals/update-request-2026-11-22/`). The quoted requests name the design doc on purpose: a first candidate that quoted "update the docs" and "atualiza a documentação" won the request as well and fired in two of eight sessions on a request to update a page that is not a design doc, where this text fired in none of eight. Routine checks of the same day on claude-sonnet-5-5, on a set that gained that request as a positive and that neighbouring request as a negative, gave the same counts before and after: 33/33 on the positives, 0/33 false fires, canary 3/3 (`README-update-clause-2026-11-22.md` there). That pair is at the ceiling and guards against a regression only. It cannot see the defect: with the document pasted and no file to edit, the old text scores 3/3 on the new positive. The description is 1013 characters, eleven under the limit `scripts/validate.py` enforces, and eight sessions measure no rate. The haiku number of the release is 80% on the ten old positives and 5/5 on the new one, with 0/33 false fires and the canary at 3/3 (claude-haiku-5-5, one sweep, 2026-11-22), against 62% two days earlier on the old text; no haiku sweep was taken on the old text the same day, so the difference is not attributed to the clause. One defect was looked at after 1.9.0 and is still open: when the user says they cannot answer now and wants the document anyway, the skill fills a template's Riscos section with risks nobody gave (a Redis dependency, the 24-hour window). `design-doc-workspace/iteration-28/` (2026-11-22, claude-sonnet-5-5, four runs per cell) found it in two of four documents with the skill installed and invoked, and in none of four when a brief tells the session to read the skill, and tried two paragraphs for step 2. Neither was adopted. The first said "or nobody is there to reply", and both of its runs then wrote the document on the plain request instead of asking first: keep those words out of the skill. The second kept the ask-first behaviour and cleaned the Riscos section in three of four, but the risk reappeared as a clause in Proposta or as an example inside the pending marker (the check for that stayed at 1/4 in both cells), and the accepted +5 ms lost its own heading in three of four. Read that iteration before writing a third.
- **structurizr** — authors/edits `workspace.dsl` (C4 model, Structurizr DSL v6+); validation is Docker-only (`structurizr/structurizr validate`), and a missing Docker means "delivered, not validated, here is the command" — never an install attempt. ADR authoring is routed to the team's decision log, not written by this skill. References split into always-read core (`dsl-reference`) plus conditional pattern files for token economy. The export commands are one of those files (`export`), so the hand-off carries only the preview. Theme tag names cited in the references are checked against the theme files the image bundles: a tag the theme does not define draws no icon and no command reports it, and the 1.6.4 example carried two (`Cloud`, `Elastic Load Balancing`) that `amazon-web-services-2025.07` had renamed.
- **mermaid-sequence** — Mermaid sequence diagrams as fenced ` ```mermaid ` blocks; never invent the flow or failure paths; technical detail (endpoint/headers/payload/status) goes in Notes. Validation is local-only and ordered: mermaid-cli Docker image → local `mmdc` → "delivered, not validated, here is the Docker command". mermaid.live may be offered for preview but it renders remotely, so for diagrams carrying internal detail that is the user's call. `references/syntax.md` is always-read (version-portability + escaping gotchas).
- **unslop** — edits prose to remove machine-writing patterns; the one skill that owns that catalog, so that other skills apply it by name instead of each carrying a copy. Rule ids are stable (`S1`–`S21` in `SKILL.md`, `EN*`/`PT*` in one vocabulary file per language under `references/`); a removed rule leaves a gap, because other skills may cite an id. Its form of the shared contract is "remove, never supply": a rule that needs a fact the text lacks deletes the claim or asks. It never edits code, diagram source, quotations, tool-parsed text, or a file that records history. **Explicit only, by its description and not by `disable-model-invocation: true`**: with that flag the Claude Code Skill tool refuses a call that comes from another skill (probed on 2026-11-21, `unslop-workspace/smoke-2026-11-21/README.md`), and the flag is not part of the Agent Skills standard, so a host that ignores it would fall back on the description anyway. The cost is that the description sits in every session's context and that "explicit" is a rate to measure, not a guarantee. The first measurement is the routine check of 2026-11-21 on claude-sonnet-5-5 (`unslop-workspace/trigger-evals/serial-2026-11-21-routine-sonnet.json`, one sweep, 3 runs per query): 0/30 false fires with the canary at 3/3, including the two boundary queries that ask for this job without naming the skill, and 21/30 on the positives. The nine misses are three queries that point at an earlier message ("the summary you just wrote", "o e-mail que eu colei acima", "unslop that"). Six captured transcripts (`transcripts-noprior-sonnet/` there) show each session answering in prose that the conversation holds no earlier text, so a single-message session cannot fire them and they say nothing about the description; the other seven positives scored 21/21. The set now carries the text in those three queries, which scored 10/10 each at ten runs with the canary at 10/10 (`serial-2026-11-21-pastedtext-probe-sonnet-n10.json`); it no longer has a query that refers to an earlier message, which this harness cannot measure, and no full sweep has been run on the new set. The eval set has 55 frozen checks (`unslop-workspace/evals/checks-baseline.json`) and a first A/B, `unslop-workspace/iteration-1/` (2026-11-21, claude-sonnet-5-5, two runs per cell): 109/110 checks met with the skill read against 98/110 without it, or 95/102 once a run that a shell alias derailed is left out. Both cells remove the tells and leave code, quotations and the accepted ADR alone; what the skill adds is on the side of "without changing its meaning and without adding a fact" (a claim made stronger in both runs without the skill, a bare assertion kept and a sentence invented in one run each). Every prompt names the skill, so the cell without it measures what the model makes of the word, and two runs measure no rate. A skill that delegates to it keeps its own short floor of prose rules for an install without `unslop`.
- **code-comments** — governs the comments of code an agent writes or changes, in any language; the trigger is "whenever you write or modify code", not a request about comments, so the `SKILL.md` body is kept short (it is read on every coding task) and the before/after pairs sit in `references/examples.md`, read only when a comment resists being made precise. The guidance on what to comment and how to word it condenses chapters 5 and 6 of *The Art of Readable Code* (Boswell & Foucher) in the skill's own words: no text and no example from the book is reproduced, and it must stay that way. Five rules are not the book's and are listed as such in `NOTICE.md`: a reason is written only when the user, the repository or the writer's own decision established it (an unknown reason is reported in the reply, never guessed in the file); comments describe the code and never narrate the edit or the conversation; the scope is the code being changed, plus any comment the change makes false; comments follow the language of the comments already in the file, then the codebase, and only then the conversation; and an existing identifier with a poor name is **not renamed**: the rename is suggested in the reply (the book says to fix the name; the skill does that only for identifiers it introduces). Its form of the shared contract is the first of those rules, and it is the one skill that does not stop to ask, because its deliverable is someone else's code change. No external tooling. The eval set (`code-comments-workspace/evals/evals.json`) has 43 frozen checks (`checks-baseline.json`, which adds the judged kind `negative`). Its first A/B is `code-comments-workspace/iteration-1/` (2026-11-21, claude-sonnet-5-5, two runs per cell): 84/86 checks met with the skill read against 79/86 without it. The one separation is eval 5, where only the skill makes the reply suggest renaming `d` without doing it (2/2 against 0/2); without the skill the model already wrote no restating or narrating comment, kept the file's language and invented no reason for a constant, and both cells gave a reason for the injectable clock in eval 6. Two runs measure no rate, and the brief told the executor to read the skill, so that A/B says nothing about triggering. The trigger set (`code-comments-workspace/trigger-evals/trigger_eval.json`) pastes the code in each query, because this repository has no code for a session to open, and six of its ten positives never mention comments. A pilot of four captured sessions (`transcripts-pilot-sonnet/` there) found the skill invoked as the first tool call or not at all, never after the code was written, so the strict count of the harness fits this skill. The routine check of 2026-11-21 on claude-sonnet-5-5 (`serial-2026-11-21-routine-sonnet.json`, one sweep, 3 runs per query) gave 0/30 false fires with the canary at 3/3, 12/12 on the four positives that name comments or docstrings, and 9/18 on the six that do not (script 3/3, bug fix 3/3, refactor 2/3, test 1/3, new function 0/3, one-line change 0/3). Three runs do not rank those six queries, as thirty captured sessions of the same day show (`transcripts-implicit-probe-sonnet-n10/`, ten per query): the test query that scored 1/3 scored 10/10; the one-line change stayed at 0/10, every session answering in prose with the changed code; the new function scored 3/10 as the first tool call, with five answers in prose, one session that invoked the skill after searching the repository and one that searched and never invoked it. That last query says "next to this one" and pastes `slugify`, a function that also exists in the eval fixtures, so two sessions went looking for the file. Reworded with nothing to look for (`dedupe_filename`, a name absent from the repository), it scored 10/10 (`transcripts-newfunction-reworded-sonnet-n10/`), and that version is the one in the set. What holds is one query: the one-line change, 0/13 over the sweep and the probe, where the session returns the changed code without consulting the skill. 1.1.0 adds a clause to the description for that case: the skill applies when the code is pasted in the message and the change is one line that looks obvious, and the clause says what comes first (the comments around the line, then the code). The form comes from `addyosmani/agent-skills`, which recorded the same one-turn answers on pasted code. It was measured on 2026-11-21 on claude-sonnet-5-5 (Claude Code 2.1.330, serial) under a rule written before the runs (`code-comments-workspace/trigger-evals/README-oneline-clause-2026-11-21.md`). Three one-line changes with the code pasted, five runs each, fired 1/15 with the 1.0.0 text and 11/15 with the clause, the canary at 4/5 and 5/5. The routine checks of the same day, the first full sweeps on the set as it now stands, gave 20/30 on the positives with the 1.0.0 text and 27/30 with the clause, with 0/30 false fires and the canary at 3/3 in both. The one-line change of the set is still the weakest query: 4/8 with the clause over the probe and the sweep, against 0/8 without it. Two of the three probe queries were written the same day as the clause, so they are not a blind holdout, and two other wordings prepared for the probe were never run, because the rule stopped at the first that passed. The description is now 1022 characters, two under the limit `scripts/validate.py` enforces. **All of those trigger numbers come from queries with the code pasted, and they do not hold when the file is in the project.** `code-comments-workspace/trigger-evals/in-project-2026-11-22/` (2026-11-22, claude-sonnet-5-5, the plugin loaded from outside the project, four sessions each on evals 1, 2, 4 and 5, none of which mentions comments) gave 0 of 16 invocations with the canary at 2/2: every session opened the file, made the change and replied. With the code pasted the session has nothing to edit and consults the skill; with the file there it edits. So in a project the skill is in practice not consulted on a plain code change, which is the case it was written for, and the 1.1.0 clause is measured only for pasted code. What is lost is what iteration-1 says the skill adds over a session without it, which is little (84/86 against 79/86, the rename suggested and not made). No change has been tried; a description in this form may not be able to win a request that never mentions comments once there is a file to edit, and a third clause would have to fit in two characters.
- **explain** — explains a topic to one reader and writes or revises texts for other people (messages, emails, replies); one skill for both because the same four questions govern them (who reads and what they know, what contrast is in play, which one or two reasons matter, what the reader does afterwards). The body is a decision procedure plus checks and **has no output template**: the research behind it found no named format (ELI5, Feynman, BLUF, ADEPT) tested against another, while it did find that instructions by adjective ("be simple", "use analogies", "be accurate") are the conditions under which the documented failures of machine-written explanations occur. So the skill instructs procedures: fix the reader from signals, choose the device by the situation, mark the limits, end on something the reader can get wrong. Decisions that are easy to undo by accident: it **explains first** at a stated assumed level and asks first only when two readers would get very different answers (a Socratic gate on a one-off question is banned; the teaching loop is opt-in); an analogy is optional, covers one aspect, and carries its mapping and its breaking point; a closing check is conditional, never a fixed ending; simplifying changes the form and keeps the scope of the claim; no effect size is stated anywhere in the skill, because several came from abstracts or secondary summaries, and no learning gain is claimed. Its form of the shared contract is "facts are recorded, illustrations are built": it is the one skill that has to build content nobody gave it (an example, an analogy, a hypothetical number), so the built parts are shown as illustrations, and it asks only when the reader or the purpose is unknown; in a text for someone else a missing fact becomes a bracketed gap listed after the text. It invokes `unslop`, when installed, only on a text it drafted for a third party: never on an explanation (S13 and S19 would strip the closing check and the analogy) and never on the user's own draft. The before/after pairs sit in `references/techniques.md` and `references/writing.md`; all were written for the skill, and the ones that echoed a source's wording or numbers were replaced. No external tooling. The eval set and the trigger eval set are written (`explain-workspace/evals/evals.json`, `explain-workspace/trigger-evals/trigger_eval.json`). # Rotate the auth service signing key

This runbook replaces the Ed25519 key the auth service uses to sign tokens. The rotation has
three phases: stage the new key, let it propagate, then promote it. The old key stays valid for
verification until the overlap window ends, so tokens signed before the promotion keep working.

Placeholders in angle brackets (`<like-this>`) are values for your environment. Fill them in
before you start.

## Before you begin

- You need write access to the secret `<secret-name>` that holds `SIGNING_KEY`.
- You need a way to restart the auth service: `<restart-command>` (for example
  `kubectl rollout restart deployment/<auth-deployment>`).
- The auth service must accept tokens signed by either `SIGNING_KEY` or `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT` while
  the rotation is in progress. Confirm this with the service owners before step 2. If the service
  only verifies with one key, promoting the new key would invalidate every token signed with the
  old one.

## 1. Generate the new key

Generate the key on a trusted workstation. Do not write the private key to a shared location or
paste it into a chat, ticket, or commit.

```bash
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out signing-key-next.pem
chmod 600 signing-key-next.pem
```

Derive the public key, which the verifiers need:

```bash
openssl pkey -in signing-key-next.pem -pubout -out signing-key-next.pub.pem
```

Delete the private key file from disk once it is stored in the secret (step 2):

```bash
shred -u signing-key-next.pem
```

## 2. Add the new key to the secret as `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT`

Store the PEM contents of `signing-key-next.pem` under `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT` in `<secret-name>`. Leave
`SIGNING_KEY` unchanged.

Check that the secret now has both keys and that `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT` is not the same as
`SIGNING_KEY`. Do not print the values.

## 3. Restart the auth service

```bash
<restart-command>
```

Wait until every replica is running and reports ready. Check that the service still issues tokens
with the current key. Tokens should still carry the old key's identifier (`<kid-or-check>`).

## 4. Wait 15 minutes

Wait 15 minutes after the restart before promoting. This gives every replica time to load
`SIGNING_KEY_NEXT` and gives clients time to pick up the new public key from `<jwks-or-public-key-location>`.

## 5. Promote the new key

Make `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT` the active signing key:

1. In `<secret-name>`, set `SIGNING_KEY` to the value of `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT`.
2. Keep the previous `SIGNING_KEY` value only while you still need it for verification. Otherwise
   remove `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT` after the promotion is verified.
3. Restart the auth service again with `<restart-command>`.

Verify that new tokens are signed with the new key (`<kid-or-check>` changes) and that existing
sessions still validate.

## 6. Clean up

- Remove `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT` from the secret once the old key is no longer needed for verification.
- Remove the old public key from `<jwks-or-public-key-location>` when the overlap window closes.
- Record the rotation date and the new key's identifier in `<rotation-log-location>`.

## Rollback

If something fails before step 5, remove `SIGNING_KEY_NEXT` from the secret and restart. Nothing
has changed for clients.

If something fails after step 5, set `SIGNING_KEY` back to the old value (keep a copy of it until
step 6), and restart.
